facts.statement: Drepanaspis is an extinct genus of armoured jawless fish that lived during the Early Devonian period, approximately 416 to 397 million years ago.
facts.quote: Drepanaspis (from 'sickle' and 'shield') is an extinct genus of heterostracan armoured jawless fish from the Early Devonian (approximately 416 - 397 mya).

facts.statement: The first fossils of Drepanaspis were found in 1887 in the Gemünden slate of Rhineland, Germany, and were first described by Clemens August Schlüter.
facts.quote: The first fossils of the genus Drepanaspis, scientifically known as D. gemuendenensis of Schlüter, were found in 1887 from the Gemünden slate in the Hunsrück lagerstätte of Rhineland, Germany and was first described by Clemens August Schlüter.

facts.statement: Scottish palaeoichthyologist Ramsay H. Traquair notably studied the fossils and created the first outline restorations of articulated Drepanaspis specimens.
facts.quote: These fossils were also most notably studied and described by Scottish palaeoichthyologist Ramsay H. Traquair who created the first outline restorations from articulated specimens of Drepanaspis.

facts.statement: In 2004, Alain Bleick and his team uncovered more Drepanaspis specimens in the Ardenne Massif of Belgium and Luxembourg, extending the geographical record to the middle-upper Emsian period.
facts.quote: More specimens of Drepanaspis would later be uncovered in 2004, in the Lower Devonian subdivision of the Ardenne Massif in Belgium and Luxembourg, specifically within the Emsian Oesling, by Alain Bleick and his team.

facts.statement: The widely spaced eyes, sensory canals, and flattened morphology of Drepanaspis suggest it was likely a bottom feeder that foraged on the ocean floor.
facts.quote: The presence of widely spaced eyes, sensory canals, and its flattened morphology suggests that these fish may have been bottom feeders that foraged the ocean floor for food.

facts.statement: Drepanaspis possesses a dorsally oriented mouth opening, a distinct feature that separates it from other heterostracan relatives.
facts.quote: Interestingly, Drepanaspis also has a dorsally oriented mouth opening which is a distinct feature that separates the genus from its other heterostracan relatives.

facts.statement: The carapace of Drepanaspis is broad, depressed, and obtusely rounded at the front, composed of overlapping ventral and dorsal plates or scales.
facts.quote: The carapace of Drepanaspis is described to be broad, depressed, and very obtusely rounded at the front, consisting of a ventral and dorsal shield made up of several overlapping plates or scales.

facts.statement: The carapace features a characteristic V-shaped pattern of tubercles, with approximately 8.5 tubercles per centimeter, which helps identify the specimen's symmetry plane.
facts.quote: These scales, or tubercles, cover a large majority of the carapace in a characteristic v-shape pattern, with approximately 8.5 tubercles per cm aligned naturally to the edge of the plate, which can be used to identify a specimen's symmetry plane.

facts.statement: Long, elongated, and pointed postero-lateral or cornual plates form most of the exterior margin of the dorsal shield along the posterior end.
facts.quote: In addition, forming most of the exterior margin of the shield along the posterior end lies long, elongated, and pointed plates called postero-lateral or cornual plates.

facts.statement: Members of Drepanaspis possess a complex lateral line sensory system consisting of closed canals within the dermal plates.
facts.quote: Like their close Heterostracan relatives, members of Drepanaspis have a sensory canal system specifically called the lateral line sensory system.

facts.statement: The lateral line sensory system in Drepanaspis likely helped detect changes in water pressure and movement, influencing its behavioral patterns.
facts.quote: These sensory organs, when found in extant species of fish, are tubes and canals rich in neuromasts shown to be important in detecting changes in water pressure and movement, along with influencing some of their behavioral patterns.

facts.statement: The diverse marine fauna found in the Gemünden slate strongly indicates that Drepanaspis was of marine origin.
facts.quote: The predominantly diverse range of marine fauna found within these slate formations strongly indicate that the members of Drepanaspis are of marine origin.

facts.statement: Observations of well-developed eyes in associated fossils suggest Drepanaspis lived in shallow offshore waters ranging from 40 to 60 meters in depth.
facts.quote: It was estimated, through observations of well-developed eyes of arthropod and vertebrate specimens recovered from the slate formation, that the water depth of the offshore environment was estimated to be rather shallow, only ranging from 40–60 meters in depth.

facts.statement: The debate over the nature of radial ridges on Drepanaspis plates continued until a specimen from the Odenspiel quarry supported W. Gross's original observation.
facts.quote: This debate would continue until the discovery of a specimen from the Odenspiel quarry in Rhineland, Germany that contained two incomplete dorsal plates, two branchial plates and several fragments of D. gemuendenensis pointing to Gross as the one with the correct observation.

facts.statement: There was initial debate regarding whether the dorsal orientation of the Drepanaspis mouth opening was natural or caused by specimen crushing.
facts.quote: Initially, there was some debate regarding the dorsal orientation of the mouth opening, specifically on whether such an orientation was natural or due to crushing of the specimen.

facts.statement: Drepanaspis is classified within the clade Drepanaspididae, which is part of the family Psammosteida.
facts.quote: Drepanaspis belongs to the clade Drepanaspididae, a subdivision of the family Psammosteida.

facts.statement: The family Psammosteida, containing Drepanaspis, belongs to the order Pteraspidiformes and the class Pteraspidomorphi, a major group within the paraphyletic Ostracodermi.
facts.quote: Psammosteida belongs to the order Pteraspidiformes and class Pteraspidomorphi, which is one of the major classes of the paraphyletic group Ostracodermi.
